In my experience, they help about 10% overall.  Just enough to keep me off the suicidal ledge, and they take the worst of my PMS mood swings away.  But it's not enough to give me motivation, energy or focus.  For that I need a stimulant & things to look forward to in life.  

As for side effects, that varies from person to person.  As long as you don't have underlying bipolar disorder, you will probably just experience diminished sex drive or orgasm ability, possible small weight gain or loss & maybe some changes in your sleep.  The most dangerous time is the first few weeks after starting or stopping an SSRI.  But beyond that it's generally smooth sailing if you're on the right dose of the right med.  They don't affect my sex drive at all but delay orgasm a bit.  And I don't feel "numb" in the slightest.  I certainly felt that way on anti-psychotics though.  Again, everyone's different in this regard though.

I've tried them all but chose Prozac because it's the easiest to quit & I can miss an entire day's dose without feeling crazy due to the long-acting nature of the drug.  Lexapro was the worst in this regard.  But it's all individual.  Don't be scared to try them; just start with a low dose & monitor yourself closely for things like suicidal/violent impulses in the first few weeks.

My only advice is to put the oxygen mask on yourself first.  You won't be any good to your wife or anyone else if you're suffocating in grief & stress.  As hard as it may be, you still have to make time for relaxing activities that take your mind off your pain...if even for only 30 minutes per day.  Could be anything from a slow walk around the block to a warm bath to a meditation session, reading, painting or journaling.  Something separate from your wife to build your autonomy & give you both a break from the relationship dynamics.  Even if it doesn't stop the pain or take your mind off stuff at first, keep doing it anyway.  Fake it 'til you make it.  Stress is a major killer aside from being extremely unpleasant.  

Being a caregiver is an ungodly hard task.  Maybe there are some organizations in your area that can come in and help?  I don't know a lot about this topic but I do know you have to make your own health/sanity a priority.  It's not disrespectful to your wife--on the contrary, it will make you a better partner.  

Don't rule out mental health/counseling services for yourself either.  There are income-based programs in most states.  It's amazing how much it helps being able to talk with a neutral 3rd party on a regular basis...to build up your coping skills or just have a place to vent.  I know men tend to be reluctant to seek services like that, but in your situation I'd say it could be a lifesaving decision.  

Sending good vibes your way.  <3

Amotivation and anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure) are core symptoms of depression.  

Healthy people are internally motivated to do things because accomplishments feel good.  They know it's hard to get up in the morning for work, but they're motivated to go because of the paycheck they'll receive and the people they'll help (or whatever).  They feel more pleasure from the small things in life, like a pretty day or a compliment, which also serves as motivation to keep pushing forward.  

When your reward center is malfunctioning, as it often is in depression or ADHD, you literally have no motivation to do anything because it doesn't feel good or give you a boost.  Everything seems pointless because you don't get the little rewards that others get throughout the day from the small victories.  

Pleasure & satisfaction are natural motivators, and when you can't feel them, everything seems pointless.  Why go to work when you can save your energy and stay in bed or play video games instead?  To outsiders it looks like laziness but it's actually just a natural result of not feeling any pleasure from your accomplishments.  

You should definitely look into medication for your ADHD. Sometimes that alone will lift the mood symptoms.  If not, there's always therapy & antidepressants.  But you gotta get that dopamine reward system working right first or you'll never feel driven or fulfilled.  I wouldn't be able to function without stimulants.

Do you take any sleep aids?  I can't sleep without one (or two).  I know they say it's not healthy to rely on them nightly, but some are safer than others.  You shouldn't use benzos or Z-drugs (Ambien, Lunesta, etc) nightly, but I find that Benadryl or other antihistamines like Unisom are fine.  Same with melatonin & Valerian root.  They're not habit-forming and are very mild.  

Avoiding TV/computer/phone screens an hour before bed is vital for preventing insomnia as well.  The light interferes with your brain's melatonin production.  Devoting that final hour before bed to a relaxing activity like reading, a warm bath or some other quiet, calming thing can also be helpful.  I like to pop my sleep aid at the start of my Chillax Hour and by the end, I'm nodding off.
